Learn about the latest scabies outbreaks in Wales, common symptoms, how the skin condition spreads, effective treatments, and ways to prevent further infection.


## Scabies Cases Reported in Wales as Hospitals Introduce Precautionary Measures


Scabies cases have been reported in several healthcare settings in Wales, prompting hospitals and residential care facilities to introduce precautionary measures to control the spread of the contagious skin condition.


According to reports published on 8 October 2026, a small number of residential homes in Carmarthenshire and hospital wards have experienced scabies outbreaks. Healthcare teams have responded by arranging treatment, restricting some visits, and implementing infection control procedures.


Although the condition can cause considerable discomfort, scabies is common and treatable. Health officials have emphasised that the reported outbreaks remain limited rather than widespread.


The developments have renewed public interest in scabies symptoms, how the infection spreads, and what people can do to protect themselves and their families.


## What Is Scabies and Why Is It Contagious?


Scabies is a contagious skin condition caused by a microscopic parasite called *Sarcoptes scabiei* . The mites burrow into the upper layer of the skin, where they live and lay eggs. This triggers an inflammatory reaction that can cause intense itching and a bumpy rash.


The infection can affect people of any age and is not a sign of poor personal hygiene. Anyone can develop scabies following close contact with an infected person.


Scabies commonly spreads through prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Household members, intimate partners, carers, and people living in residential facilities may face a higher risk because they have frequent close contact with others.


The mites can also spread through recently contaminated clothing, towels, and bedding, although this is less common with ordinary scabies than direct physical contact.


Because symptoms may take several weeks to appear after the initial infection, someone can have scabies before realising they have it. This delay can make identifying and controlling an outbreak more challenging.


## Latest Scabies Outbreak Reports in Welsh Hospitals


Recent reports have highlighted scabies cases at healthcare facilities in Wales, where infection prevention teams have introduced measures to reduce transmission.


At Bronllys Hospital near Brecon, an outbreak was identified on Llewelyn Ward. Visitor restrictions were introduced after a small number of patients were found to have the condition.


Hospital staff and affected patients were offered treatment as part of efforts to prevent additional cases. Healthcare representatives described the steps as precautionary measures intended to protect patients, employees, and visitors.


Separately, scabies cases were reported in a small number of residential homes in Carmarthenshire, according to Hywel Dda University Health Board.


Prince Philip Hospital in Llanelli also experienced scabies-related restrictions in September. Subsequent reports stated that Wards 4 and 7 had completed the required environmental cleaning and reopened. However, restrictions remained in place at the Mynydd Mawr Rehabilitation Unit at the time covered by the report.


The health board also noted that some patients were arriving at hospital with scabies acquired in the community, highlighting that not every case is necessarily linked to a hospital outbreak.


These developments demonstrate why healthcare facilities take even relatively small outbreaks seriously, particularly when patients may be vulnerable or require close personal care.


## Common Scabies Symptoms to Watch For


Recognising the early signs of scabies can help people seek treatment and reduce the risk of passing the infection to others.


The most common symptom is intense itching, which often becomes worse at night. A rash may also develop, appearing as small red spots, bumps, or irritated patches of skin.


Scabies commonly affects areas such as:


- Between the fingers and around the wrists
- The elbows and armpits
- The waist and abdomen
- The buttocks and groin
- Areas around the nipples
- The feet and ankles


In infants and young children, symptoms may also affect the scalp, face, palms, and soles of the feet.


Some people develop thin, raised lines on the skin where mites have burrowed. However, these marks can be difficult to see, and symptoms may resemble eczema or other skin conditions.


According to the NHS, symptoms can take up to eight weeks to appear following a first infestation. People who have had scabies previously may notice symptoms sooner.


Anyone experiencing persistent itching or an unexplained rash, particularly after close contact with someone who has scabies, should seek advice from a pharmacist or GP.


## How Is Scabies Treated?


Scabies can usually be treated effectively with medication designed to kill the mites. Depending on the person's circumstances, a pharmacist or healthcare professional may recommend a medicated cream or lotion.


Treatment must be used according to the product instructions or professional advice. Some treatments require application over the entire body, including areas that do not show visible symptoms. The exact application instructions vary by product and age group.


A second application may be necessary after seven days, depending on the recommended treatment.


It is particularly important for household members and other close contacts to receive treatment at the same time when advised. Treating only the person with visible symptoms can allow the infection to circulate between people.


Bedding, towels, and recently worn clothing should also be handled according to NHS guidance. Items that can be washed should be washed at 60°C or above where suitable. Items that cannot be washed may need to be sealed in a bag for several days, following official advice.


People should avoid close physical contact until the recommended initial treatment period has passed. Anyone unsure about when it is safe to return to work, school, or normal activities should follow advice from their healthcare professional.


Children under two years old with suspected scabies should be assessed by a GP rather than treated with an ordinary pharmacy product without professional guidance.


## Why Can Itching Continue After Treatment?


One of the most frustrating aspects of scabies is that itching can continue for several weeks after successful treatment.


This does not necessarily mean that the mites are still present. The skin may continue reacting to the mites and their products even after the infestation has been treated.


However, persistent symptoms can sometimes indicate reinfection, incorrect application, or treatment failure.


Seek medical advice if itching continues for two to four weeks after treatment has finished, if new burrows or rashes appear, or if the skin becomes increasingly painful, swollen, or infected.


A thick, crusted, or flaky rash, particularly on the hands, feet, elbows, or knees, also warrants prompt medical assessment because it may indicate a more severe form of scabies.


## How to Reduce the Risk of Scabies Spreading


Preventing further transmission requires coordinated action, particularly in households, hospitals, and residential care facilities.


Practical steps include:


- Seek medical or pharmacy advice promptly if scabies is suspected.
- Complete the full treatment course as directed.
- Ensure household members and close contacts are treated simultaneously when recommended.
- Avoid sharing clothing, towels, and bedding.
- Wash suitable clothing and bedding used shortly before treatment.
- Follow advice about avoiding close physical contact after treatment begins.
- Inform healthcare facilities if you have suspected or confirmed scabies before visiting.


People with unexplained rashes or suspected scabies should contact healthcare providers for advice before visiting vulnerable patients.


Scabies is generally treatable, and appropriate infection control measures can help limit its spread.


## Conclusion


Recent reports of scabies outbreaks in Welsh hospitals and residential care settings have highlighted the importance of recognising symptoms and seeking timely treatment.


Although scabies can cause severe itching and discomfort, it is not usually associated with serious illness and can generally be treated successfully.


Understanding how the infection spreads, treating close contacts when advised, and following hygiene and infection control guidance can help prevent further transmission.


Anyone concerned about persistent itching, an unexplained rash, or possible exposure should contact a pharmacist or GP for appropriate advice.
